title: Methodology
section: Cleaning: how each event is identified
text:
Cleaning: how each event is identified

Free throws drawn are credited to the free-throw shooter. Play-by-play logs the fouler on the foul row, not the fouled player.
Three-shot fouls: “free throw 1 of 3” trips. The fouled missed three is not logged as an attempt, so the denominator is three-point attempts plus three-shot trips.
And-ones: a “1 of 1” free throw by a player who made a field goal at the same game-clock moment (98% of all 1-of-1 trips; most of the rest are away-from-play and, since 2022-23, transition take fouls).
Self-creation: a made field goal with no assist credited.
Heaves (36+ feet with ≤ 3 seconds left in a period) are excluded everywhere. From 2025-26 the NBA logs missed heaves as team attempts, so excluding them keeps all seasons on one definition.
The 2012-13 season was missing its final 16 games in the primary archive. They were restored from the older-format feed using an event-code mapping learned from the 1,213 games present in both.

title: Methodology
text:
The expected-FG (xFG) model
To reward making hard shots, we first need to know how hard each shot was. The xFG model estimates the probability that a shot goes in from where and how it was taken: location, distance, angle, zone, shot family (jumper, layup, dunk, hook, tip), whether it came off a drive or on the move, period, game clock and season. It never sees who took the shot, otherwise it would absorb the very skill we are trying to measure.
Shot-type labels get more detailed over time (9 types in 1996-97, 50 by 2007-08; “step-back” and “pull-up” don’t exist early on), so the model uses five shot families that exist in every season.
The model is gradient-boosted trees (xgboost) trained on 5,841,268 shots from 1996-97 to 2023-24 (6,307,970 in total), tuned on 2024-25, and evaluated on the held-out 2025-26 season:

Excess free-throw rate is the key whistle metric. Rim-attackers should shoot more free throws, so a regression predicts each player’s shooting-foul free-throw rate from shot diet (rim, paint, mid-range, corner-three and three-point shares), a usage proxy, and position, fitted separately for each era with season fixed effects. The residual, free throws beyond what that profile earns, is the excess. This separates a center finishing through contact from a guard manufacturing fouls on jumpers.
Only shooting-foul free throws count. Intentional fouls (hack-a-big, fouling a good free-throw shooter late in a close game) are the defense’s strategy, not the shooter’s foul-seeking, and would otherwise penalize elite free-throw shooters for being fouled on purpose.

title: Methodology
text:
Shrinkage, standardization, and the composite

Empirical-Bayes shrinkage. A 1,000-minute season still contains only a few dozen three-shot fouls or and-ones, so raw rates for small samples produce fake extremes. Each count rate is shrunk toward its season mean with a beta-binomial prior; continuous measures (shot-making, difficulty, excess FT rate) use a normal-normal prior. Priors are estimated each season from players with reliable samples.
Within-season z-scores. Every component is standardized against the same season’s qualifying scorers, which neutralizes era-wide shifts (the 2004-05 hand-check removal, the three-point boom, league-wide whistle trends). Each component’s z is capped at ±4 so no single metric can dominate.
Two axes. Skill Score and Whistle Score are the weighted means of their components’ z-scores, each re-standardized within season.
EHI = 0.4 × Skill − 0.6 × Whistle, re-standardized within season and mapped to 0–100 (50 = average qualifier, 15 points = one standard deviation).
Archetypes come from the signs of the two axes: Ethical Hooper (skill ≥ 0, whistle < 0), Whistle Artist (skill ≥ 0, whistle ≥ 0), Downhill Bully (skill < 0, whistle ≥ 0), Grinder (skill < 0, whistle < 0).


Why these weights

Whistle outweighs skill (60% / 40%). In the slang, an ethical hooper doesn’t have to be the most skilled player, but they cannot live at the line.
Shot-making above expected gets the largest skill weight because it is the most direct measure of skill net of shot selection. Self-creation captures handles and shot creation. Difficulty and footwork are supporting signals.
Excess FT rate gets the largest whistle weight because it is the cleanest whistle measure net of shot diet. Three-point fouls are the purest jump-shot foul-drawing signal available back to 1996-97. FT share of points captures raw free-throw reliance relative to scoring volume. Perimeter and-ones are noisier, so they get the least weight.

title: Methodology
text:
Who qualifies
A hooper is a real scorer: a regular-season player-season qualifies with ≥ 1,000 minutes (prorated in the shortened 1998-99, 2011-12, 2019-20 and 2020-21 seasons) and ≥ 12 field-goal attempts per 36 minutes. Role players who rarely shoot shouldn’t top the “ethical” list by default. Playoffs use ≥ 150 minutes. Careers need ≥ 4 qualifying seasons. Career EHI is the minutes-weighted average; peak EHI is the best minutes-weighted three-consecutive-qualifying-season stretch.

That yields 4,022 regular-season and 1,302 playoff player-seasons, and 417 careers.

title: Methodology
text:
Changes from the original design
Each was triggered by a result that looked wrong, checked against the data, and documented in the project’s NOTES.md:

“Share of and-ones on jumpers” became perimeter and-ones per 100 perimeter attempts. The share version mostly measured shot diet (it tracked a player’s share of jump shots closely), so a pure spot-up shooter whose handful of and-ones all came on jumpers looked like a foul-baiter.
Free-throw metrics use shooting-foul free throws only, removing intentional fouls (see above).
Usage is approximated by scoring attempts per 36 minutes, since true usage rate needs team possession data from the blocked stats server. Within-season standardization makes the two nearly equivalent.
Whistle weighted 60/40 over skill, reflecting the slang definition.

title: Methodology
text:
Limitations

No defender distance before 2013-14. xFG knows where and how a shot was taken, not how well it was contested. A player who takes many tightly-contested shots will look like a better shot-maker than one who takes open looks from the same spots.
Missed-shot fouls can only be located for threes. Play-by-play records a shooting foul on a missed two but not where the shot was, so jump-shot foul-baiting on twos is only visible through and-ones and the excess-FT residual.
Officiating varies by crew, season and arena. Within-season standardization removes league-wide shifts but not crew-to-crew noise.
Flopping is only recorded in play-by-play from 2023-24 and is too sparse to use.
Style, not morality. Drawing fouls is legal and frequently smart. A low EHI means a player scored differently, not wrongly.

title: Eras
text:
How the whistle changed


Three-point foul-drawing exploded and then got policed. Three-point shooting fouls rose from 0.77 per 100 attempts in 1996-97 to a peak of 1.82 in 2016-17, the peak of the leg-kick, lean-into-the-closeout era. They fell to 1.08 in the first crackdown season.
Shooting-foul free throws per shot went from 0.225 (1996-97) to 0.196 (2020-21) and 0.212 (2025-26).
Self-created offense has receded. The unassisted share of made field goals peaked at 43.6% (2009-10) and stands at 36.3% today, as offenses move the ball more.
Travels and offensive fouls have fallen from 2.92 to 1.76 per 100 scoring attempts.

title: The Ethical Hooper Index
text: Every pickup run has one: the player who never seems to need a whistle. No arm-hooks, no launching sideways into a closeout, no head-snap on contact. Just footwork, a jumper, and a bucket. Basketball has a name for that player: the ethical hooper. This project turns the slang into a number.

title: The Ethical Hooper Index
text:
What is an ethical hooper?

An ethical hooper is a player who scores and dominates through pure skill, clean footwork, natural shot-making, and fluid movement, rather than trickery, flopping, or foul-baiting.

No rule manipulation. They don’t jump into defenders, hook arms, or sell contact with exaggerated head-snaps to earn a whistle.
An aesthetic playstyle. Their offense runs on clean mid-range pull-ups, pure jump shots, smooth handles, and honest post moves.
Low free-throw reliance. They take few free throws relative to their scoring volume, beyond what their shot diet would naturally earn.


In measurable terms: an ethical hooper generates scoring through skill rather than the whistle: high shot-making relative to shot difficulty, self-created offense, clean footwork, and low dependence on free throws that are not explained by an aggressive, rim-attacking shot diet. A center who lives at the rim should shoot free throws. A guard who draws three-shot fouls by leaning into closeouts is a different story.

This is a stylistic metric, not a moral judgment of any person. It uses on-court play-by-play data only. Drawing fouls is legal and often smart basketball. The index describes how a player scores, nothing about who they are.







Look up any player: the Player Search page charts a player’s Ethical Hooper Index season by season.

title: The Ethical Hooper Index
text:
The map
The index has two axes. Skill Score (x) blends shot-making above expectation, self-creation, shot difficulty, and clean footwork. Whistle Score (y, flipped so “clean” is up) blends excess free throws, three-point fouls drawn, free-throw share of points, and perimeter and-ones. Every value is measured against the same season’s peers, so a 1999 post-up big and a 2025 pull-up guard are compared on equal footing.

The Ethical Hooper Index (EHI) combines both axes on a 0–100 scale where 50 is an average qualifying scorer. Because the slang is mostly about not living at the line, the whistle axis carries 60% of the weight and skill 40%. An ethical hooper doesn’t have to be the most skilled player on the floor, just a clean one.

title: The Ethical Hooper Index
text:
Top-line findings


Steve Nash is the most ethical hooper of the last 30 years (career EHI 87.7 over 8 qualifying seasons), combining elite shot-making (+2.76 SD) with a light whistle (-1.17 SD). James Harden ranks last of 417 qualifying careers (EHI 10.7, Whistle Score +3.60 SD).
The style is a real, persistent trait. A player’s EHI correlates r = 0.74 with their EHI the next season (2,708 season pairs).
The NBA’s 2021-22 crackdown on “non-basketball moves” left a visible mark. League-wide, three-point shooting fouls fell from 1.42 to 1.08 per 100 attempts in one season. Players our index had flagged as whistle-dependent lost efficiency afterward: each standard deviation of pre-rule Whistle Score predicted a 0.38-point drop in true shooting (p = 0.049), while a placebo “rule” in 2019-20 shows nothing (p = 0.814).
Ethical hoopers are common. 117 of 417 careers land in the Ethical Hooper quadrant, including Payton Pritchard, Nikola Vučević and Chris Paul.
In 2025-26, the cleanest qualifying scorers were Bobby Portis, Payton Pritchard and Jrue Holiday.

title: The 2021-22 Crackdown
text:
Before the 2021-22 season, the NBA told officials to stop rewarding “non-basketball moves”: abrupt sideways or backward launches into defenders, hooking a defender’s arm, and similar tricks designed to draw a foul rather than score. It is the closest thing basketball has to a policy experiment on exactly the behavior this index measures.
League-wide, the effect was immediate: three-point shooting fouls fell from 1.42 to 1.08 per 100 attempts in one season. The sharper question is whether the rule hit the players who had been leaning on those moves, and whether our index had flagged them in advance.

title: The 2021-22 Crackdown
text:
Before the 2021-22 season, the NBA told officials to stop rewarding “non-basketball moves”: abrupt sideways or backward launches into defenders, hooking a defender’s arm, and similar tricks designed to draw a foul rather than score. It is the closest thing basketball has to a policy experiment on exactly the behavior this index measures.
League-wide, the effect was immediate: three-point shooting fouls fell from 1.42 to 1.08 per 100 attempts in one season. The sharper question is whether the rule hit the players who had been leaning on those moves, and whether our index had flagged them in advance.

title: The 2021-22 Crackdown
text:
Design

Panel: regular-season player-seasons with 500+ minutes, 2018-19 to 2025-26. The minutes threshold deliberately ignores shot volume, so the sample isn’t filtered on the outcomes being measured. Treated players are those who were qualifying scorers before the rule (237 players).
Pre-period 2018-19 to 2020-21; post-period 2021-22 to 2025-26.
Treatment intensity: each player’s pooled pre-period three-point shooting-foul rate, standardized (continuous), plus a binary top-quartile version. An alternative uses the index’s own pre-period Whistle Score.
Specification: two-way fixed effects (player + season) difference-in-differences with standard errors clustered by player (fixest). Season effects absorb the league-wide drop, so estimates measure the differential change for heavier foul-drawers.

title: The 2021-22 Crackdown
section: The trap: regression to the mean
text:
The trap: regression to the mean
Players picked because they drew unusually many fouls in 2018-21 will tend to draw fewer later even with no rule change. Extreme seasons don’t repeat. Two checks separate the rule from that drift:

Placebo: pretend the rule arrived in 2019-20, measuring treatment in 2016-18 and using only pre-rule seasons. Any “effect” there is pure drift.
Separate treatment window: measure foul-drawing in 2016-18, before the outcome window, so mean reversion can’t mechanically create the effect.

Three-point fouls: mostly drift
The headline estimate looks dramatic: each standard deviation of pre-rule foul-drawing predicts -0.53 three-point fouls per 100 attempts afterward (p < 0.001). But the placebo shows -0.38 (p < 0.001) with no rule at all, and measuring treatment in the earlier window shrinks the effect to -0.17 (p = 0.168). Most of the apparent targeting is regression to the mean. The rule clearly lowered three-point fouls for everyone, but this design can’t show it fell disproportionately on the prior foul-drawers.



Efficiency: a real, targeted hit
True shooting tells a cleaner story. Heavier pre-rule foul-drawers lost 0.83 TS points per standard deviation after the rule (p < 0.001). The effect survives every check:

the early treatment window (0.55 points, p = 0.010), so it is not mean reversion;
an age control (0.61 points, p < 0.001), so it is not aging foul-drawers;
while the placebo is flat (-0.05 points, p = 0.814).




The index saw it coming
Using the pre-rule EHI Whistle Score as the treatment, a measure built before and independently of the rule, each standard deviation of whistle-dependence predicts a 0.38-point drop in true shooting after the crackdown (p = 0.049). The players the index labeled as whistle-reliant are the ones whose scoring got less efficient once the league stopped rewarding non-basketball moves. That is external validation of what the Whistle Score measures.
The excess free-throw rate did not fall differentially (+0.003, p = 0.490). One reading: foul-drawers still got to the line on drives and contact at the rim, but lost the cheap jump-shot whistles that had padded their efficiency.

title: The 2021-22 Crackdown
text:
Caveats

Event-study pre-trends look flat partly by construction, because treatment is measured over the same pre-period. The placebo and early-window checks carry the identification weight.
The sample is small (237 players), and the binary top-quartile group even smaller.
Linear age is absorbed by player + season fixed effects; the age control is a quadratic term.
Other things changed after 2021-22 (pace, the take-foul rule in 2022-23). They hit all players, and season fixed effects absorb anything common to everyone.

title: Validation
text:
4. Predictive validation: the 2021-22 rule change
The strongest test of a “whistle” measure is whether it predicts what happens when the league takes the whistle away. Players with higher pre-2021 Whistle Scores lost 0.38 points of true shooting per standard deviation after the crackdown (p = 0.049), while a placebo rule date shows no effect. Full analysis on the Rule Change page.

Bugs caught by these checks (now fixed):

Intentional fouls inflated the free-throw rates of elite free-throw shooters (fouled on purpose late in games) and poor ones (hack-a-big). Now only shooting-foul free throws count.
“And-ones on jumpers” as a share flagged pure spot-up shooters as foul-baiters. It’s now a rate per perimeter attempt.
Shrinkage priors were briefly distorted by tiny samples, producing |z| > 8 outliers. They’re now fit on reliable samples only.
Shot-chart joins, the 2012-13 missing games, and heave logging changes were all caught during the data audit, before any metric was built.

How to read it. Skill Score blends shot-making above expected, self-creation, shot difficulty and clean footwork. Whistle Score blends excess free throws, three-point fouls drawn, free-throw share of points and perimeter and-ones. Both are in standard deviations versus that season’s qualifying scorers. See Methodology. This is a stylistic measure of how a player scores, not a judgment of the person.
